items.stem: Why does scarcity exist?
items.answer: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
items.markingKey: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited. Even rich societies face scarcity.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Opportunity cost is the total of all the things you gave up." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is only the single next best alternative, not all the alternatives combined.
items.markingKey: It is only the single next best alternative, not all the alternatives combined. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana has one free Saturday and enough money for only one of these: buying a novel, saving for a laptop or a new pair of trainers. Ana ranks them in that order of preference and chooses buying a novel. What is the opportunity cost of this choice? Explain.
items.answer: Saving for a laptop – the next best alternative forgone
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = the next best alternative given up = saving for a laptop (1); not all the alternatives combined and not the money price (1).

items.stem: Explain why "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into scarcity, needs and wants and opportunity cost.
items.answer: It applies opportunity cost to a familiar context and can be investigated with a survey.
items.markingKey: It applies opportunity cost to a familiar context and can be investigated with a survey. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Using all its resources, a factory in Bangladesh can produce either 190 units of shirts or 130 units of bags per year (a straight-line production possibility curve). What is the opportunity cost of producing one unit of bags? If it produces 90 units of bags, what is the maximum amount of shirts it can produce?
items.answer: 1.46 units of shirts; 58.5 units of shirts
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost of 1 bags = 190 ÷ 130 = 1.46 shirts (M1 A1); shirts = 190 − 1.46×90 = 58.5 (A1).

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why the production possibility curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: With fixed resources, producing more of one good means moving resources away from the other good, so less of the other can be produced.
items.markingKey: Content: With fixed resources, producing more of one good means moving resources away from the other good, so less of the other can be produced. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Design a 10-question survey; collect 30 responses; record spending categories; ask for the next best alternative given up; calculate percentages; present in a pie chart; evaluate honesty and sample size.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Design a 10-question survey; collect 30 responses; record spending categories; ask for the next best alternative given up; calculate percentages; present in a pie chart; evaluate honesty and sample size. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Opportunity cost is the most useful idea in economics."
items.answer: It is one of the most fundamental ideas because scarcity makes every choice a trade-off, but it is most useful alongside other tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it applies to every decision by individuals, firms and governments; it reminds decision-makers to consider alternatives. Arguments against: other ideas, such as supply and demand, explain how markets set prices; the value of the next best alternative is often hard to measure. Supported judgement: It is one of the most fundamental ideas because scarcity makes every choice a trade-off, but it is most useful alongside other tools. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Briefly explain why every choice involves an opportunity cost.
items.answer: Because resources are scarce, using them for one thing means they cannot be used for the next best alternative, which is given up.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Because resources are scarce, using them for one thing means they cannot be used for the next best alternative, which is given up. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a need and a want.
items.answer: A need is essential for survival (food, water, shelter); a want is desirable but not essential (a new phone). What counts as a need can vary between societies.
items.markingKey: A need is essential for survival (food, water, shelter); a want is desirable but not essential (a new phone). What counts as a need can vary between societies. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to the COVID-19 vaccine roll-out in 2021, explain how it illustrates scarcity and allocation.
items.answer: With limited doses, governments chose which groups to vaccinate first, such as older people and health workers. Scarce vaccines meant every priority choice delayed protection for someone else.
items.markingKey: Context (With limited doses, governments chose which groups to vaccinate first, such as older people and health workers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: scarce vaccines meant every priority choice delayed protection for someone else. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to scarcity and allocation.

items.stem: Sana is investigating scarcity, needs and wants and opportunity cost and proposes the research question: "Is money important?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed, vague value question Improved: "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed, vague value question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do students at our school decide how to spend their weekly pocket money, and what do they give up?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: What reward does the factor "enterprise" earn?
items.answer: Profit
items.markingKey: Profit. Land earns rent, labour wages, capital interest.

items.stem: Mateo has one free Saturday and enough money for only one of these: a new pair of trainers, a train trip to the coast or saving for a laptop. Mateo ranks them in that order of preference and chooses a new pair of trainers. What is the opportunity cost of this choice? Explain.
items.answer: A train trip to the coast – the next best alternative forgone
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = the next best alternative given up = a train trip to the coast (1); not all the alternatives combined and not the money price (1).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why education is described as an investment in human capital.
items.answer: It increases workers' skills and knowledge, so they become more productive and can earn more in the future, just as investment in machines increases output. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It increases workers' skills and knowledge, so they become more productive and can earn more in the future, just as investment in machines increases output. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which tea production in Kenya shows how to produce: labour-intensive methods.
items.answer: Much Kenyan tea is still hand-picked by large numbers of workers on hillside estates and smallholdings. Abundant labour and steep terrain make labour-intensive production sensible.
items.markingKey: Context (Much Kenyan tea is still hand-picked by large numbers of workers on hillside estates and smallholdings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: abundant labour and steep terrain make labour-intensive production sensible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how to produce: labour-intensive methods.

items.stem:
Source A – Business report (paraphrased): Summary of news reports on mechanisation of tea picking in Kericho, Kenya, 2010s–2020s

A survey of tea estates found that hand-picking remains common because skilled pickers select only the top leaves, giving higher-quality tea. Some estates have introduced picking machines, which cut costs but have led to protests by workers worried about losing their jobs.

What is the message of Source A about the factors of production and the three economic questions? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: Kenyan tea estates face a choice between skilled hand-picking and cheaper machines that threaten jobs.
items.markingKey: Kenyan tea estates face a choice between skilled hand-picking and cheaper machines that threaten jobs. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Labour is the most important factor of production."
items.answer: Labour is essential, especially skilled labour, but production depends on combining all four factors; their importance varies by industry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every good and service needs human effort and ideas; education and skills (human capital) drive long-run growth. Arguments against: without land and capital labour produces little; enterprise is needed to organise production. Supported judgement: Labour is essential, especially skilled labour, but production depends on combining all four factors; their importance varies by industry.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "land"?
options: The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise
The amount of output produced per worker or per unit of input
The basic economic problem that human wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited
All natural resources, such as soil, minerals, water and forests
items.answer: All natural resources, such as soil, minerals, water and forests
items.markingKey: D. "land" is all natural resources, such as soil, minerals, water and forests.

items.stem: "Machines always replace workers and reduce jobs." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Machines can replace some jobs but also raise productivity, lower prices and create new jobs, for example in maintenance and design.
items.markingKey: Machines can replace some jobs but also raise productivity, lower prices and create new jobs, for example in maintenance and design. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on the factors of production and the three economic questions produced the question "What are factors of production?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it only asks for a definition Improved: "Why do some coffee farms in Colombia use labour-intensive methods while large farms in Brazil use machines?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it only asks for a definition); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why do some coffee farms in Colombia use labour-intensive methods while large farms in Brazil use machines?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Business report (paraphrased): Summary of news reports on mechanisation of tea picking in Kericho, Kenya, 2010s–2020s

A survey of tea estates found that hand-picking remains common because skilled pickers select only the top leaves, giving higher-quality tea. Some estates have introduced picking machines, which cut costs but have led to protests by workers worried about losing their jobs.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the factors of production and the three economic questions. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of news reports on mechanisation of tea picking in Kericho, Kenya, 2010s–2020s. Purpose: to report on economic change and its impact on workers. Value: It shows the trade-off between labour and capital in a real industry and includes workers' concerns. Limitation: News reports may focus on conflict and do not give full data on costs or how many estates use machines.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of news reports on mechanisation of tea picking in Kericho, Kenya, 2010s–2020s. Purpose: to report on economic change and its impact on workers. Value: It shows the trade-off between labour and capital in a real industry and includes workers' concerns. Limitation: News reports may focus on conflict and do not give full data on costs or how many estates use machines. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "command (planned) economy".
items.answer: An economy in which the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an economy in which the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "The United States is a pure market economy with no government involvement." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The US is a mixed economy: government provides defence, roads, public schools, Medicare and regulates many markets.
items.markingKey: The US is a mixed economy: government provides defence, roads, public schools, Medicare and regulates many markets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why command economies often suffered shortages.
items.answer: Planners could not gather enough information about what people wanted; prices did not signal demand, and managers aimed to meet targets rather than satisfy consumers. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Planners could not gather enough information about what people wanted; prices did not signal demand, and managers aimed to meet targets rather than satisfy consumers. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How did the introduction of the household responsibility system after 1978 affect farm output in China?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Collect grain-output data (1975–1990) from FAO or World Bank; read two secondary sources; draw a line graph; compare before and after; consider other factors (prices, fertiliser); cite sources.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect grain-output data (1975–1990) from FAO or World Bank; read two secondary sources; draw a line graph; compare before and after; consider other factors (prices, fertiliser); cite sources. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Zara argues that "A market economy is the best way to answer the three economic questions." Nia disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Markets are effective at producing most goods, but the evidence from most successful economies supports a mixed system with government correcting market failures.
items.markingKey: Zara: prices give signals that allocate resources efficiently. Nia: markets underprovide public goods and can ignore pollution. Judgement (1-2 marks): Markets are effective at producing most goods, but the evidence from most successful economies supports a mixed system with government correcting market failures.

items.stem:
Source A – Government statement (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a saying of Deng Xiaoping (from 1961, widely quoted during China's reforms after 1978)

The leadership declared that it did not matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice: what mattered was whether a policy developed the economy, not whether it was labelled socialist or capitalist.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about economic systems: traditional, command, market and mixed. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of a saying of Deng Xiaoping (from 1961, widely quoted during China's reforms after 1978). Purpose: to justify pragmatic economic reforms that introduced market elements. Value: It captures the reasoning used by China's leaders to move towards a mixed economy. Limitation: It is a political slogan, not evidence of how reforms worked in practice or who benefited.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of a saying of Deng Xiaoping (from 1961, widely quoted during China's reforms after 1978). Purpose: to justify pragmatic economic reforms that introduced market elements. Value: It captures the reasoning used by China's leaders to move towards a mixed economy. Limitation: It is a political slogan, not evidence of how reforms worked in practice or who benefited. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "private sector"?
options: Income that is not spent and is kept for future use
The part of the economy owned and run by the government, such as state schools and hospitals
A plan of expected income and spending over a period of time
The part of the economy owned and run by individuals and private businesses for profit
items.answer: The part of the economy owned and run by individuals and private businesses for profit
items.markingKey: D. "private sector" is the part of the economy owned and run by individuals and private businesses for profit.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a market economy and a command economy.
items.answer: In a market economy private owners make decisions through prices and profit; in a command economy the state owns resources and planners decide output and prices.
items.markingKey: In a market economy private owners make decisions through prices and profit; in a command economy the state owns resources and planners decide output and prices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why "How did the introduction of the household responsibility system after 1978 affect farm output in China?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into economic systems: traditional, command, market and mixed.
items.answer: It examines a real transition between economic systems using output data.
items.markingKey: It examines a real transition between economic systems using output data. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A market economy is the best way to answer the three economic questions."
items.answer: Markets are effective at producing most goods, but the evidence from most successful economies supports a mixed system with government correcting market failures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prices give signals that allocate resources efficiently; competition encourages innovation and choice. Arguments against: markets underprovide public goods and can ignore pollution; they can leave poor people without essentials, increasing inequality. Supported judgement: Markets are effective at producing most goods, but the evidence from most successful economies supports a mixed system with government correcting market failures. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Compound interest is interest paid on…
items.answer: the original sum and on interest already earned
items.markingKey: the original sum and on interest already earned. Interest earns interest.

items.stem: Explain the difference between compound interest and simple interest.
items.answer: Simple interest is paid only on the original sum; compound interest is paid on the original sum plus the interest already added.
items.markingKey: Simple interest is paid only on the original sum; compound interest is paid on the original sum plus the interest already added. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why making a budget can help a young person save for a goal.
items.answer: It shows exactly where money goes, separates needs from wants, and sets a realistic amount to save each month towards the target.
items.markingKey: Content: It shows exactly where money goes, separates needs from wants, and sets a realistic amount to save each month towards the target. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Is saving good?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into personal finance: budgeting, saving and spending decisions. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed value question with an obvious answer Improved: "How do students in Grade 8 at our school plan and track their spending, and does planning lead to more saving?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed value question with an obvious answer); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do students in Grade 8 at our school plan and track their spending, and does planning lead to more saving?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Arjun can save €2,500 for 2 years in Account A (2.5% simple interest) or Account B (2.5% interest compounded annually). Calculate the interest earned in each account and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: A: 2,500 × 0.025 × 2 = €125.00 (A1). B: 2,500 × (1 + 0.025)^2 − 2,500 = €126.56 (M1 A1). B earns more because interest is paid on previous interest (compounding) (R1).

items.stem: Explain why making a budget can help a young person save for a goal.
items.answer: It shows exactly where money goes, separates needs from wants, and sets a realistic amount to save each month towards the target.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows exactly where money goes, separates needs from wants, and sets a realistic amount to save each month towards the target. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – Survey summary (paraphrased): Summary of OECD, PISA Financial Literacy results, 2022 assessment (published 2024)

An international survey of 15-year-olds found that, on average across participating countries, about one in five students did not reach the baseline level of financial literacy, meaning they could not, for example, recognise the value of a simple budget.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about personal finance: budgeting, saving and spending decisions. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of OECD, PISA Financial Literacy results, 2022 assessment (published 2024). Purpose: to compare countries' financial-literacy education and inform policy. Value: It comes from a large international organisation using a standard test across many countries. Limitation: Only some countries took part, and a test cannot capture all real-life money behaviour.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of OECD, PISA Financial Literacy results, 2022 assessment (published 2024). Purpose: to compare countries' financial-literacy education and inform policy. Value: It comes from a large international organisation using a standard test across many countries. Limitation: Only some countries took part, and a test cannot capture all real-life money behaviour. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem:
Source A – Survey summary (paraphrased): Summary of OECD, PISA Financial Literacy results, 2022 assessment (published 2024)

An international survey of 15-year-olds found that, on average across participating countries, about one in five students did not reach the baseline level of financial literacy, meaning they could not, for example, recognise the value of a simple budget.

"Schools should teach personal finance as a compulsory subject." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Agree that it should be taught to everyone, but it can be built into existing subjects rather than added as a separate course.
items.markingKey: From the source: Many teenagers lack basic financial skills, so financial education is needed. Own knowledge for: many young people make costly mistakes with credit and debt; budgeting and saving skills improve lifelong well-being. Own knowledge against: families and part-time work already teach money skills; the curriculum is crowded and the content can be included in maths and I&S. Judgement: Agree that it should be taught to everyone, but it can be built into existing subjects rather than added as a separate course. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made"?
items.answer: opportunity cost
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of opportunity cost.

items.stem: Oil under the North Sea is an example of which factor of production?
items.answer: Land
items.markingKey: A. All natural resources count as land.

items.stem: Which country has the clearest example of a command economy today?
items.answer: North Korea
items.markingKey: D. The state controls almost all production.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Saving money at home is just as good as saving in a bank." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Money at home earns no interest and loses value to inflation; it can also be lost or stolen.
items.markingKey: Money at home earns no interest and loses value to inflation; it can also be lost or stolen. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Scarcity means a good has run out." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants; goods can be scarce even if shops are full.
items.markingKey: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants; goods can be scarce even if shops are full. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between capital-intensive production and labour-intensive production.
items.answer: Labour-intensive production uses many workers relative to machines (e.g. tea picking in Kenya); capital-intensive production uses many machines relative to workers (e.g. car assembly in Japan).
items.markingKey: Labour-intensive production uses many workers relative to machines (e.g. tea picking in Kenya); capital-intensive production uses many machines relative to workers (e.g. car assembly in Japan). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the private sector and the public sector.
items.answer: The public sector is owned and run by the government to provide services; the private sector is owned by individuals and firms seeking profit.
items.markingKey: The public sector is owned and run by the government to provide services; the private sector is owned by individuals and firms seeking profit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why saving early is especially powerful.
items.answer: Compound interest means interest is earned on earlier interest, so money saved earlier grows for longer and builds up faster.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Compound interest means interest is earned on earlier interest, so money saved earlier grows for longer and builds up faster. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sana has one free Saturday and enough money for only one of these: saving for a laptop, going to a football match or a cinema trip with friends. Sana ranks them in that order of preference and chooses saving for a laptop. What is the opportunity cost of this choice? Explain.
items.answer: Going to a football match – the next best alternative forgone
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = the next best alternative given up = going to a football match (1); not all the alternatives combined and not the money price (1).

items.stem: Using all its resources, a farm in New Zealand can produce either 190 units of rugs or 100 units of pottery per year (a straight-line production possibility curve). What is the opportunity cost of producing one unit of pottery?
items.answer: 1.9 units of rugs
items.markingKey: Giving up all 190 rugs gains 100 pottery, so 1 pottery costs 190 ÷ 100 = 1.9 rugs (M1 A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Which economic system is best?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into economic systems: traditional, command, market and mixed. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad and evaluative, with no place, period or criteria Improved: "How did the introduction of the household responsibility system after 1978 affect farm output in China?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad and evaluative, with no place, period or criteria); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How did the introduction of the household responsibility system after 1978 affect farm output in China?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh shows credit and personal finance.
items.answer: Founded by Muhammad Yunus in 1983, it gives small loans mainly to poor women, who repay in weekly instalments. Small loans with group support can help people start businesses, though high interest can also cause debt.
items.markingKey: Context (Founded by Muhammad Yunus in 1983, it gives small loans mainly to poor women, who repay in weekly instalments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: small loans with group support can help people start businesses, though high interest can also cause debt. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to credit and personal finance.

items.stem:
Source A – Economics textbook definition (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Lionel Robbins, "An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science", 1932

Economics is the study of how people allocate scarce resources that have alternative uses. Because resources can be used in many ways, every decision to use them in one way means giving up the chance to use them in another.

items.answer: Economics is about choices with scarce resources that have alternative uses.

items.stem: Mohammed argues that "Labour is the most important factor of production." Rafael disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Labour is essential, especially skilled labour, but production depends on combining all four factors; their importance varies by industry.
items.markingKey: Mohammed: every good and service needs human effort and ideas. Rafael: without land and capital labour produces little. items.stem: Sana earns S$2,300 a month after tax and spends: rent S$800, food S$350, transport S$150, phone and internet S$100, leisure S$270. (a) Calculate the monthly saving and the savings rate as a percentage of income. (b) How many whole months will it take to save S$6,500 for a deposit on a course? (c) Suggest one change to the budget, justified as a need or a want.
items.markingKey: (a) S$2,300 − S$1,670 = S$630 (A1); 630 ÷ 2,300 × 100 = 27.4% (A1). (b) 6,500 ÷ 630 = 10.32 → 11 months (round up) (M1 A1). (c) e.g. reduce leisure (a want) rather than rent or food (needs) (R1).

items.stem:

How reliable is Source A for someone researching scarcity, needs and wants and opportunity cost? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Lionel Robbins, "An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science", 1932. Purpose: to define the subject of economics for students and scholars. Value: It is a classic, widely quoted definition from a leading economist. items.stem:

A survey of tea estates found that hand-picking remains common because skilled pickers select only the top leaves, giving higher-quality tea. Some estates have introduced picking machines, which cut costs but have led to protests by workers worried about losing their jobs.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Labour is the most important factor of production."
items.answer: Labour is essential, especially skilled labour, but production depends on combining all four factors; their importance varies by industry.

items.stem:
Source A – Government statement (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a saying of Deng Xiaoping (from 1961, widely quoted during China's reforms after 1978)

The leadership declared that it did not matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice: what mattered was whether a policy developed the economy, not whether it was labelled socialist or capitalist.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "A market economy is the best way to answer the three economic questions."
items.answer: Markets are effective at producing most goods, but the evidence from most successful economies supports a mixed system with government correcting market failures.
items.markingKey: From the source: Economic results matter more than ideology, justifying market reforms. Own knowledge for: prices give signals that allocate resources efficiently; competition encourages innovation and choice. Own knowledge against: markets underprovide public goods and can ignore pollution; they can leave poor people without essentials, increasing inequality. items.stem: A street vendor in Dhaka borrows 200 US dollars from a microfinance institution at a flat interest rate of 18% per year for 6 months. Calculate the total amount repaid and the equal monthly repayment.
items.answer: Total $218.00; monthly $36.33

items.stem: Define the term "production possibility curve (PPC)".
items.answer: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "factors of production".
items.answer: The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which country used five-year plans from 1928 under Stalin?
items.answer: The Soviet Union
items.markingKey: The Soviet Union. The plans set targets for industry.

items.stem: Explain the difference between fixed expenses and variable expenses.
items.answer: Fixed expenses stay the same each period (rent, phone contract); variable expenses change (food, entertainment).
items.markingKey: Fixed expenses stay the same each period (rent, phone contract); variable expenses change (food, entertainment). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the production possibility curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: With fixed resources, producing more of one good means moving resources away from the other good, so less of the other can be produced.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With fixed resources, producing more of one good means moving resources away from the other good, so less of the other can be produced. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Amara has one free Saturday and enough money for only one of these: a train trip to the coast, a cinema trip with friends or going to a football match. Amara ranks them in that order of preference and chooses a train trip to the coast. What is the opportunity cost of this choice? Explain.
items.answer: A cinema trip with friends – the next best alternative forgone
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = the next best alternative given up = a cinema trip with friends (1); not all the alternatives combined and not the money price (1).

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "The United States is a pure market economy with no government involvement." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The US is a mixed economy: government provides defence, roads, public schools, Medicare and regulates many markets.
items.markingKey: The US is a mixed economy: government provides defence, roads, public schools, Medicare and regulates many markets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Buying something on sale always saves money." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It only saves money if you would have bought it anyway; otherwise you spend money you would have kept.
items.markingKey: It only saves money if you would have bought it anyway; otherwise you spend money you would have kept. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ingrid has one free Saturday and enough money for only one of these: going to a football match, a cooking class or buying a novel. Ingrid ranks them in that order of preference and chooses going to a football match. What is the opportunity cost of this choice? Explain.
items.answer: A cooking class – the next best alternative forgone
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = the next best alternative given up = a cooking class (1); not all the alternatives combined and not the money price (1).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "Why do some coffee farms in Colombia use labour-intensive methods while large farms in Brazil use machines?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect information from FAO and coffee-industry reports on farm size, terrain and wages; compare in a table; interview a coffee importer or read case studies; evaluate sources; cite in APA.

items.stem: With reference to Maasai pastoralism in Kenya and Tanzania, explain how it illustrates a traditional economy.
items.answer: Many Maasai communities have traditionally herded cattle, with land managed collectively and roles set by age and gender, though many now also take part in markets and tourism. Custom has long decided what to produce and how, but outside pressures are changing it.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Opportunity cost is the most useful idea in economics." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: It is one of the most fundamental ideas because scarcity makes every choice a trade-off, but it is most useful alongside other tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it applies to every decision by individuals, firms and governments; it reminds decision-makers to consider alternatives. Thesis/conclusion: It is one of the most fundamental ideas because scarcity makes every choice a trade-off, but it is most useful alongside other tools.
